learning.focus: Build a thick soup from beans and bread without scorching it.
learning.outcome: Tender greens and whole beans in a creamy bread-thickened soup, finished with fragrant olive oil.
before: Start soaking the beans 12 hours before making the soup, then plan an overnight chill after layering it with bread.
Use a large soup pot and a separate bean pot; the original batch contains more than a kilogram of greens before they wilt.
Choose plain bread made without milk or eggs if cooking for a vegan table.

checkpoints.cue: The beans have boiled vigorously for at least 30 minutes and are creamy all the way through after simmering.
checkpoints.why: Cannellini are white kidney beans; a full boil in fresh water addresses their lectin hazard, and tenderness determines when they are ready to purée.

checkpoints.cue: The potato pieces yield easily to a knife and the bean purée thickens the liquid.
checkpoints.why: Bread will absorb more liquid overnight, so the first-day soup must remain wet enough to soak it.

checkpoints.cue: The reheated soup reaches at least 165°F throughout and a full boil, then bubbles gently without catching underneath.
checkpoints.why: Starchy soup heats unevenly and scorches readily; stirring distributes heat.

troubleshooting.problem: The soup catches on the bottom.
troubleshooting.cause: Bean purée and bread make it thick, especially during reheating.
troubleshooting.fix: Lower the heat, stir along the entire base and add a little water until it moves freely; transfer to a clean pot if it has burned.

troubleshooting.cause: Their age and storage affect the cooking time.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue simmering the beans, keeping them submerged, before making the soup; do not use the clock alone.

learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours, or within 1 hour above 90°F, and keep at 40°F or colder. Use within 3–4 days of the first cooking; reheating does not restart that clock. Reheat to 165°F throughout. The required overnight chill is part of that storage period. Freeze cooled portions for longer keeping; thaw in the refrigerator and reheat gently with a little water.
learning.timing: Plan two preparation days: 12 hours to soak, roughly 2–3 hours for the beans and soup, an overnight chill, and 10–20 minutes to heat the soup fully and bring it to a full boil before its final 10-minute simmer. These are planning ranges. At another batch size, choose enough pot and shallow-container capacity; soaking and cooling rules and tenderness cues stay the same.

ingredients: water, enough for soaking, then fresh water to keep the beans generously covered while cooking
extra-virgin olive oil, enough to coat the bottom of the soup pot
400 g cavolo nero (Tuscan kale), tough stems removed, leaves cut into strips
500 g savoy cabbage, cored and cut into strips
200 g chard, leaves sliced; tender stems chopped separately
2 potatoes, peeled and cut into small, even pieces
hot water, as needed to keep the vegetables simmering in liquid
500 g stale plain bread, sliced; traditionally Tuscan unsalted bread
water, only as needed to loosen the chilled soup
extra-virgin olive oil, for drizzling over each bowl

exactAfter.body:
## Chef's Note

The bread is part of the soup, soaking up the bean broth overnight before the second simmer gives ribollita its thick, spoonable texture. Cavolo nero, savoy cabbage and chard each bring something different; keep the full mixture and finish each bowl with good olive oil. This follows the Accademia’s Tuscan formula, with refrigerated soaking and overnight storage.

## Directions

1. **Soak and cook the beans:** Use dried cannellini beans and water to soak the beans for 12 hours in the refrigerator. Drain and discard the soaking water. Put the beans in a separate pot with fresh water generously covering them. Bring to a rolling boil for at least 30 minutes, then simmer until completely tender and creamy inside, topping up with hot water to keep them submerged. Allow roughly 1–2 hours of cooking in total; older beans can take longer. Keep the beans in their cooking liquid.
2. **Start the soup:** Put extra-virgin olive oil, onions, carrots, and celery ribs in a large, heavy soup pot over medium-low heat. Cook, stirring, until the vegetables soften without darkening, about 10–15 minutes.
3. **Add the vegetables:** Add tomatoes, cavolo nero (Tuscan kale), savoy cabbage, chard, and potatoes, putting the chard stems in before the leaves. Stir the greens in by handfuls as they wilt. Use a pot that can hold all the vegetables and bean liquid with room to stir; split the soup between pots if necessary.
4. **Thicken with beans:** Pass a generous half of the cooked beans through a sieve into their reserved cooking liquid, keeping the rest of the beans whole. Add the purée and its liquid to the vegetables. Have hot water, salt, and black pepper ready. Simmer gently for about 1 hour, stirring along the bottom and adding water whenever needed to prevent scorching. The potatoes and greens should be tender and the broth thickened by the puréed beans. Stir in the reserved whole beans just before taking the pot off the heat, then season to taste.
5. **Layer and chill:** Use all the stale plain bread to make two layers in several shallow heatproof containers: bread, half the soup, more bread, then the remaining soup. Divide the bread and soup between the containers evenly enough that each contains both. Refrigerate promptly within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F; do not leave the soup out overnight. Chill at 40°F or colder until the next day.
6. **Simmer again and serve:** Have water and extra-virgin olive oil ready. Transfer the chilled soup to a heavy pot. Warm gently with frequent stirring along the bottom; if too thick to stir, loosen it with a little water. Check that it reaches 165°F throughout and bring it to a full boil while stirring along the bottom, then reduce to a gentle bubbling simmer for about 10 minutes. Spoon into bowls and finish with the olive oil.

wholeRecipeReview.allocations: 400 g beans assigned to one preparation destination, then all cooked beans reappear as source-supported puréed generous-half and remaining whole beans; no invented dried-weight split. All 500 g bread is used across the two layers. All vegetables and tomato go into the soup. Independent oil allowances represent sauté and raw drizzle; cooking, soup and reheating water each have a destination.
wholeRecipeReview.ratios: Bread/dried-bean mass ratio 500/400=1.25; specified greens total 1,100 g, 2.75 times dried-bean weight. Six portions therefore represent a hearty bread-and-bean soup, not a light cup of broth. Water volume and final cooked yield are intentionally unmeasured.
wholeRecipeReview.capacity: A separate bean pot and large soup pot must accommodate all greens before wilting plus beans and their broth, with stirring headroom. No invented liter size or tested fit; additional pots permitted. Multiple shallow containers preserve layered composition and enable cooling.
wholeRecipeReview.ingredientState: Dried beans, fresh greens and vegetables, stale plain bread; trimmed/torn greens and small even potato pieces clarify handling. Bread's unsalted Tuscan style is a regional recommendation, not a gram conversion.
wholeRecipeReview.heatDoneness: Rolling fresh-water bean boil then creamy tender center; gentle soup simmer until potatoes and greens tender; reheated thick soup reaches 165°F throughout before source's 10-minute simmer.
wholeRecipeReview.schedule: 12-hour soak, roughly 2–3 hours first-day cooking, overnight refrigerator hold, 20–30-minute final heat/simmer. About 28–40-hour elapsed window is an authored planning estimate.
wholeRecipeReview.storage: First-cooking storage clock includes overnight; rapid shallow refrigeration at 40°F maximum, 3–4 days total and 165°F reheating.
